name: Hajar
line: Left with her baby in an empty valley, her search for water gave the world Zamzam.
story: Ibrahim left Hajar and baby Ismail in the barren valley of Makkah with a bag of dates and a skin of water. She asked if Allah had commanded it; when he said yes, she said, "Then He will not abandon us." When the water ran out she ran seven times between Safa and Marwah, and the spring of Zamzam burst out.
legacy: Every pilgrim who walks between Safa and Marwah repeats her steps.
lesson: Trust in Allah and effort go together: she trusted, and she still ran.
note: The Quran alludes to her in Ibrahim's prayer (14:37) but does not name her; her story is told by Ibn Abbas in al-Bukhari.

name: Jurayj
line: A monk falsely accused of fathering a child, cleared when the newborn baby spoke.
story: Jurayj was praying in his hermitage when his mother called, and he kept praying. She prayed he would not die before facing the faces of immoral women. A woman later accused him of fathering her child, and the people wrecked his hermitage. Jurayj prayed, then asked the baby who his father was. The baby answered: the shepherd.
lesson: A mother's call carries great weight, and Allah defends the innocent.
note: One of three babies the Prophet ﷺ said spoke in the cradle: Isa, the baby in Jurayj's story, and a baby in a third story. Also reported by Muslim.

name: The boy of the trench
role: The boy who would not bend
line: A boy who gave his life so a whole people would believe in Allah.
story: A king sent a boy to learn sorcery, but on the way he learned true faith from a monk. Allah cured the sick through his prayers, and the king could not kill him from a mountain or at sea. The boy told him: gather the people and shoot me, saying "In the name of Allah, Lord of the boy." He died, and the crowd cried out that they believed.
legacy: Surah al-Buruj remembers the believers who were then thrown into trenches of fire.
lesson: Victory can mean your message living on, not you.
note: The hadith names no place or people. Ibn Ishaq places it in Najran and names the boy Abdullah ibn al-Thamir; scholars differ on whether it is the same event as Dhu Nuwas's massacre.

name: The monk of the trench
line: A monk who taught the boy true faith and was killed for refusing to give it up.
story: On his way to the sorcerer, the boy sat with a monk and learned the worship of Allah. When the boy told him of his miracles, the monk said, "Today you are better than me, and you will be tested." The king seized him and ordered him to abandon his religion. He refused and was sawn in two.
lesson: A quiet teacher can shape a hero, then stand firm himself.
note: Unnamed in the hadith.

name: The king of the trench
line: A tyrant who killed the boy, then threw believers into trenches of fire.
story: The king tried every way to kill the boy and failed, until he followed the boy's own instructions and said "In the name of Allah, Lord of the boy." The people believed at once. In rage, he had trenches dug and fires lit, and threw in everyone who would not turn back.
lesson: Force can kill believers but cannot kill belief.
note: Unnamed in the hadith. Some commentators identify him with Dhu Nuwas of Himyar; others keep the two stories apart.

name: The three men in the cave
line: Three travellers trapped by a rock, freed one by one through their most sincere deeds.
story: A rock sealed three men inside a cave. Each called on Allah by a deed done only for Him: one had waited all night with milk for his sleeping parents, one walked away from sin with his cousin out of fear of Allah, and one grew a worker's forgotten wage into a herd and gave it all back. With each prayer the rock moved, until they walked free.
lesson: Deeds done in secret for Allah are what you can call on in a crisis.
note: Also reported by Muslim. Not the same as the People of the Cave in Surah al-Kahf.

name: The man who killed a hundred
line: A killer of a hundred people who died walking toward repentance and was forgiven.
story: A man who had killed ninety-nine people asked a monk if he could repent. The monk said no, so he killed him too. A scholar told him yes, and to leave for a land of people who worship Allah. He died on the way. The angels of mercy and punishment disputed over him; the land was measured, and he was a little closer to the good town.
lesson: No sin is bigger than Allah's mercy, and repentance means changing where you stand.
note: Also reported by Muslim. The story also shows the danger of answering religious questions without knowledge.
aliases: the man who killed a hundred

name: The leper, the bald man and the blind man
line: Three men healed and made rich; only one remembered where his blessing came from.
story: Allah sent an angel to three men of Bani Israil. He cured the leper, the bald man and the blind man, and gave them camels, cows and sheep. Years later the angel returned looking like a poor traveller and asked for help. The first two denied they had ever been poor. The once-blind man said, "Take what you like." Allah was pleased with him and angry with the others.
lesson: Gratitude is shown by giving, not by remembering to say thanks.
note: Also reported by Muslim.

name: The woman and the cat
line: A woman who entered the Fire for locking up a cat until it starved.
story: The Prophet ﷺ told of a woman who shut a cat away, neither feeding it nor letting it hunt for itself, until it died. For that cruelty she entered the Fire. In some reports he said he saw her during his prayer at the solar eclipse.
lesson: Cruelty to animals is a sin Allah takes seriously.
when: A woman of an earlier time (undated)
note: Also reported by Muslim. Some versions describe her as a woman of Bani Israil, another as a woman of Himyar.

name: The woman who gave water to a dog
line: A sinful woman forgiven by Allah because she gave water to a thirsty dog.
story: A dog was circling a well, almost dead from thirst. A prostitute of Bani Israil saw it, took off her leather sock, drew water with it and let the dog drink. Allah forgave her for that act of mercy.
lesson: Never think a small kindness is too small, or a sinner beyond mercy.
note: Also reported by Muslim. A similar hadith tells of a man who did the same and was forgiven.

name: The man who lent a thousand dinars
line: Two men took Allah as their only witness, and the sea delivered the debt.
story: A man of Bani Israil asked to borrow a thousand dinars. For witness and guarantor, he said Allah is enough. When the debt fell due he found no boat, so he sealed the money and a note in a hollow log and threw it into the sea. The lender, waiting on the shore, picked up the log for firewood and found his money.
lesson: Keep your word even when no one can force you to.
note: The borrower later came with another thousand dinars, and the lender told him Allah had already delivered it.

name: The man who asked his sons to burn him
line: A man so afraid of meeting Allah that he asked to be burned and scattered.
story: A man who had done little good told his sons: when I die, burn me and scatter my ashes on the wind and sea. They did. Allah gathered him whole and asked why he had done it. He said, "Out of fear of You, my Lord." And Allah forgave him.
lesson: Sincere fear of Allah is itself a door to His mercy.
note: Also reported by Muslim. Scholars explain he was excused through ignorance, not that doubting Allah's power is acceptable.

name: The jar of gold
role: Two honest men and a judge
line: A buyer and seller of land who both refused a jar of gold they found.
story: A man bought land and found a jar of gold buried in it. He tried to return it to the seller. The seller said, "I sold you the land and all that is in it." They went to a judge, who learned one had a son and the other a daughter. He told them to marry the two and spend the gold on them and in charity.
lesson: Honesty on both sides turned a dispute into a wedding.
note: Also reported by Muslim.

name: The man whose charity went astray
line: A man who gave charity three nights running, each time to the wrong person.
story: A man resolved to give charity in secret. The first night it went to a thief, the next to an immoral woman, the third to a rich man, and each morning people mocked him. Yet he said, "Praise be to Allah." He was told it was accepted: perhaps the thief would stop stealing, the woman would turn back, and the rich man would learn to give.
lesson: Allah rewards the sincere intention, not only the outcome.
note: Also reported by Muslim.

name: The merchant who forgave debts
line: A trader who told his staff to go easy on poor debtors, and Allah went easy on him.
story: A merchant used to lend to people. When his collectors found someone in hardship he told them, "Let it go, perhaps Allah will let us go." When he met Allah, Allah forgave him.
lesson: Treat others the way you hope Allah will treat you.
note: Reported by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

name: Barsisa
line: A devout monk led step by step by Shaytan into murder and disbelief.
story: A monk known for worship was left to look after a sick woman. Shaytan led him on, one small step at a time, until he sinned with her, killed her to hide it, and finally bowed to Shaytan to escape punishment. Then Shaytan disowned him, as Surah al-Hashr describes.
lesson: Great falls are made of small steps; guard against the first one.
note: The story is told by early commentators under 59:16; it is likely from Israelite lore, and the name comes from the commentators, not the Quran or sound hadith.

name: The last man to enter Paradise
line: The last man out of the Fire, given a Paradise ten times the size of the world.
story: The Prophet ﷺ described a man crawling out of the Fire who keeps asking for a little more, promising each time it will be his last request. Finally Allah tells him to enter Paradise, and gives him the like of the world and ten times more. The man asks, "Are You mocking me, while You are the King?" and the Prophet ﷺ laughed as he told it.
lesson: If the least in Paradise receives this, imagine the rest.
note: Narrated by Ibn Mas'ud; reported by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

name: The Jassasa
line: A hairy creature on a far island who led shipwrecked sailors to a chained man.
story: Tamim al-Dari told the Prophet ﷺ how storms drove his ship to an island for a month. A creature so hairy they could not tell front from back, the Jassasa, led them to a man bound in chains. He asked about the palms of Baysan and the unlettered prophet, then said he was the Dajjal. The Prophet ﷺ had the story told from the minbar.
lesson: The Prophet ﷺ confirmed news that matched his warnings, from whoever brought it.
note: Tamim al-Dari is a Companion and lives in the companions file. The island's location is not known.

name: Ibn Sayyad
line: A boy in Madinah with strange claims, whom some Companions thought was the Dajjal.
story: Ibn Sayyad was a youth in Madinah who claimed visions. The Prophet ﷺ tested him, hiding a word in his mind; he could only stammer "al-dukh". Umar asked to kill him, but the Prophet ﷺ said: if he is the one, you will not be given power over him; if not, there is no good in killing him.
lesson: Even with a suspect, the Prophet ﷺ judged by evidence, not fear.
when: Madinah, in the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime
note: Reported by al-Bukhari and Muslim. Companions differed over whether he was the Dajjal; Tamim's account of the chained man on the island points elsewhere. Later reports say he became Muslim.

name: Adnan
line: Forefather of the Prophet ﷺ, the furthest point of his agreed lineage.
story: Adnan is the ancestor of the northern Arab tribes, descended from Ismail. The genealogists agree on the Prophet's ﷺ lineage back to Adnan. Between Adnan and Ismail, the names and number of generations are disputed.
legacy: Quraysh, Kinanah, Tamim and many tribes trace back to him.
note: Dates are unknown; genealogists warned against relying on names above Adnan.

name: Fihr ibn Malik
line: The ancestor most genealogists say gave the tribe of Quraysh its name.
story: Fihr ibn Malik was a forefather of the Prophet ﷺ, and many genealogists say he was the one called Quraysh. Every clan of Quraysh, from Banu Hashim to Banu Umayyah, descends from him.
note: Others say Quraysh was al-Nadr ibn Kinanah. His dates are not known.

name: Amr ibn Luhay
line: The chief of Makkah who first changed the religion of Ibrahim and set up idols.
story: Amr ibn Luhay of Khuza'ah ruled Makkah after Jurhum. Tradition says he saw idols in Syria and brought them back, starting idol worship around the Kaaba, and invented the custom of setting animals free for idols. The Prophet ﷺ said he saw him in the Fire, dragging his intestines.
legacy: Over the centuries, Makkah filled with 360 idols until the Prophet ﷺ cleared them in 630.
lesson: One leader's innovation can mislead a people for generations.
note: The vision of him in the Fire is reported by al-Bukhari and Muslim; the details of bringing idols from Syria come from Ibn Ishaq and the historians.

name: Qusayy ibn Kilab
line: The ancestor who brought Quraysh into Makkah and took charge of the Kaaba.
story: Qusayy gathered the scattered clans of Quraysh and settled them around the Kaaba, taking its keys from Khuza'ah. He built Dar al-Nadwa, the council house, and organised the duties of Makkah: water and food for pilgrims, the Kaaba's keys, and the war banner.
legacy: His sons and grandsons, including Hashim, inherited these duties down to the Prophet's ﷺ family.
note: Dates are rough estimates by historians from generation counts.

name: Abd Manaf
line: Son of Qusayy and father of Hashim, Abd Shams, al-Muttalib and Nawfal.
story: Abd Manaf, son of Qusayy, became the leading figure of Quraysh. His sons founded clans that shaped Islamic history: Hashim, the Prophet's ﷺ clan, and Abd Shams, from whom the Umayyads came.
legacy: Both the Prophet's ﷺ family and the Umayyad caliphs trace back to him.
note: His given name is reported as al-Mughirah. Dates are not known.

name: Hashim ibn Abd Manaf
line: Great-grandfather of the Prophet ﷺ, who fed Makkah in famine and began the trade journeys.
story: His name was Amr; he was called Hashim, "the one who crumbles", because he broke bread into broth for his people in a famine. He is credited with starting Quraysh's winter caravan to Yemen and summer caravan to Syria. He married Salma of Yathrib and died on a journey at Gaza.
legacy: His clan, Banu Hashim, is the Prophet's ﷺ family.
note: Linking Surah Quraysh's two journeys to Hashim comes from the historians and commentators. Dates are estimates.

name: Abd al-Muttalib
line: Chief of Makkah who rediscovered Zamzam and faced Abraha's elephant army.
story: Named Shaybah, he was raised in Yathrib and brought to Makkah by his uncle al-Muttalib. He dug out the lost well of Zamzam. When Abraha came to destroy the Kaaba, he asked only for his camels, saying, "The House has a Lord who will protect it." He raised his orphan grandson Muhammad ﷺ until he died when the boy was eight.
legacy: At Hunayn the Prophet ﷺ called out, "I am the son of Abd al-Muttalib."
note: His vow to sacrifice a son, ransomed with 100 camels, and the camel exchange with Abraha come from Ibn Ishaq. The Hunayn saying is reported by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

name: Abdullah ibn Abd al-Muttalib
line: The father of the Prophet ﷺ, who died before his son was born.
story: Abdullah was the son his father had vowed to sacrifice; tradition says the lot fell on him and he was ransomed with a hundred camels. He married Aminah bint Wahb, then left with a trade caravan to Syria. On the way back he fell ill and died in Yathrib, months before Muhammad ﷺ was born.
note: Most historians say he died before the birth; a minority say shortly after.

name: Aminah bint Wahb
line: Mother of the Prophet ﷺ, who died when he was six.
story: Aminah, of the Zuhrah clan of Quraysh, was widowed before her son was born. When he was six she took him to visit relatives in Yathrib, and on the way home she fell ill and died at al-Abwa. Barakah Umm Ayman brought the boy back to Makkah. Decades later the Prophet ﷺ visited her grave and wept.

name: Thuwaybah
line: A freedwoman of Abu Lahab who nursed the baby Muhammad ﷺ before Halimah.
story: Thuwaybah nursed the newborn Muhammad ﷺ for a few days, and had also nursed his uncle Hamzah and Abu Salamah, making them his milk brothers. The Prophet ﷺ honoured her and sent her gifts all her life.
note: Whether she accepted Islam is disputed among historians.

name: Halimah al-Sa'diyyah
line: The Bedouin nurse who took the orphan no one wanted, and found her life full of blessing.
story: Halimah of Banu Sa'd came to Makkah in a year of drought on a weak donkey, and took the orphan baby because no richer child was left. From then on, her milk, her camel and her flock flourished. He grew up in the desert with her family, and there, as a boy, his chest was opened by Jibril.
lesson: The child others passed over was the greatest blessing of all.

place.name: Lands of Banu Sa'd, near Ta'if

note: The blessings of her journey are told by Ibn Ishaq; the opening of the chest is in Muslim. Whether she lived to accept Islam is disputed.

name: Bahira
line: A Christian monk who saw signs of prophethood in a twelve-year-old boy.
story: When the young Muhammad ﷺ travelled to Syria with Abu Talib's caravan, the monk Bahira, who usually ignored traders, came out to meet them. He had noticed signs around the boy and recognised him from his books. He told Abu Talib to take him home and guard him well.
when: About 582 CE, when the Prophet ﷺ was about twelve
note: Al-Tirmidhi grades it hasan gharib; scholars such as al-Dhahabi doubted some details in it. The name Bahira comes from Ibn Ishaq.

name: Nastur
line: A monk who said only a prophet had ever rested beneath that tree.
story: On the trade journey he led for Khadijah, the young Muhammad ﷺ rested under a tree near a monk's cell in Syria. The monk Nastur asked Maysarah who he was, and said no one but a prophet had ever sat under that tree. Maysarah carried the story home to Khadijah.
note: Reported by Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Sa'd, not in the major hadith books.

name: Maysarah
line: The servant whose report of the journey to Syria moved Khadijah to propose.
story: Khadijah sent her servant Maysarah with Muhammad ﷺ when he led her caravan to Syria. Maysarah came back full of praise: for his honesty in trade, his manners, and what the monk Nastur had said. The profit was double, and soon after Khadijah proposed marriage.
note: From Ibn Ishaq. Nothing reliable is known of whether he lived to see Islam.

name: Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl
line: A Makkan who refused idols and searched for the religion of Ibrahim before Islam.
story: Zayd would lean against the Kaaba and say, "O Quraysh, none of you follows the religion of Ibrahim but me." He would not eat meat sacrificed to idols, rescued baby girls their fathers meant to bury, and travelled to Syria seeking the true faith. He died a few years before the revelation began.
legacy: His son Sa'id ibn Zayd became one of the ten promised Paradise.
note: He was a cousin of Umar ibn al-Khattab. The year of his death is approximate.

name: Quss ibn Sa'ida
line: An Arab sage remembered for preaching one God at the fair of Ukaz.
story: Quss ibn Sa'ida of Iyad was famed as the finest speaker of the Arabs. He is remembered standing on a camel at the fair of Ukaz, telling the crowds that all who live must die, and that there is a God greater than their idols. Later reports say the Prophet ﷺ remembered hearing him.
note: The reports of the Prophet ﷺ mentioning him are weak (da'if); his fame as an orator is well attested in Arabic literature.

name: Waraqa ibn Nawfal
line: Khadijah's Christian cousin, who recognised the first revelation as the message of Musa.
story: After the first revelation in Hira, Khadijah took the shaken Prophet ﷺ to her cousin Waraqa, an old, blind Christian who had studied the scriptures. Waraqa said, "This is the same Namus that Allah sent to Musa," and wished he would live to support him when his people drove him out. He died soon after.
note: "Namus" here is understood as Jibril, the keeper of secrets.

name: Abu Talib
line: The uncle who raised the Prophet ﷺ and shielded him from Quraysh for forty years.
story: Abu Talib took his orphaned nephew in at eight and took him on caravans to Syria. When Quraysh demanded he give him up, he refused, and he endured the years of boycott in the valley with Banu Hashim. As he lay dying in 619, the Prophet ﷺ begged him to say there is no god but Allah. The reports say he died on the religion of Abd al-Muttalib.
legacy: His son Ali ibn Abi Talib became the fourth caliph.
lesson: Guidance is in Allah's hand alone, even for those we love most.
when: Died 619 CE, the Year of Sorrow
note: Al-Bukhari reports 28:56 was revealed about him. Mainstream Sunni scholars hold he did not die a Muslim; the Shia view differs.

name: Ashama the Najashi
line: A Christian king who sheltered the first Muslim refugees and wept at Surah Maryam.
story: When Muslims fled Makkah in 615, the Najashi of Aksum received them. Quraysh sent envoys to demand them back, but after Jafar ibn Abi Talib recited Surah Maryam, he wept and said this and what Isa brought came from the same source. He refused to hand them over. When he died, the Prophet ﷺ prayed the funeral prayer for him in Madinah.
legacy: The first hijrah succeeded because one king was just.
lesson: Justice opens doors that power cannot.
when: Hosted the Muslims from 615; died about 630 CE (9 AH)
note: Linking 3:199 and 5:83 to him comes from the commentators. Muslim reports the Najashi who received the Prophet's letter later was not the one he prayed over.
title: Negus

name: Salman's teachers
line: A chain of Christian monks who passed Salman along until the last pointed him to Arabia.
story: Salman left his Persian home to follow Christianity, serving one monk after another in Syria, Mosul, Nusaybin and Amorium. As each died he named the next. The last told him a prophet would soon appear in a land of palms between two lava fields, who would accept gifts but not charity and bear a seal between his shoulders.
legacy: Salman found every sign in Madinah and became a great Companion.
note: Salman's own account is reported by Ahmad in the Musnad with a sound chain. The monks are unnamed. Salman al-Farisi lives in the companions file.

name: Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt
line: A poet of Ta'if who preached one God in verse, yet would not follow the Prophet ﷺ.
story: Umayyah of Thaqif read the old scriptures and filled his poems with Allah, the angels and the Hereafter. He is said to have hoped he would be the coming prophet, and pride kept him from following Muhammad ﷺ. The Prophet ﷺ liked his poetry and said, "He nearly became Muslim."
lesson: Knowing the truth is not enough without the humility to follow it.
note: "He nearly became Muslim" is reported by al-Bukhari and Muslim. Some commentators linked 7:175 to him; others to an Israelite, Bal'am.

name: Uways al-Qarani
line: A Yemeni the Prophet ﷺ never met, yet told Umar to ask for his prayers.
story: The Prophet ﷺ described a man from Yemen, of the tribe of Qaran, who had been cured of leprosy except a coin-sized spot, and who was devoted to his mother. He told Umar: if you can, ask him to pray for your forgiveness. Years later Umar found him among the Yemeni troops and did just that.
lesson: Caring for a parent can raise someone unknown to the highest rank.
note: Many reports say he was killed at Siffin in 657, but this is not certain.
